Accordions and tabs drawn while they open

Five more controls from ui-feed.dev, rebuilt with HTML-in-canvas. Each one shows and hides content: two accordions, an order summary that expands, and two sets of tabs. Under the drawings are <details> elements and <input type="radio">s. I wanted to know if a canvas could draw a <details> closing, when a closed one has no content left to draw, and how far the picture of an element can be stretched before it looks wrong.

Credit: every control on this page is a rebuild of a demo on ui-feed.dev, and each section links to the original it came from. The originals are far higher fidelity than these, so go and look at them. These are examples of what HTML-in-canvas makes possible with a native element underneath, not replacements. I worked from the published demos rather than their source: I looked at what each one does, worked out the mechanism and built it again. The designs and the ideas are theirs.

Fragrance notesCoast path mapOrder summary Bus stop timetableKinetic poster

Fragrance notes

Three <details>, one open at a time. The canvas draws each one as a picture and clips it to as much of its notes as are open so far, so a section slides shut while the next one opens. The plus sign and the rules are drawn by the canvas. Tap the open section to close it. The sections are <option> children, with the notes in data-notes. The bottle is drawn once, on a plain canvas, and copied in each frame.

Coast path map

Five legs of a walk, each a <details>, and one is always open. Tap a leg and its map unfolds on four panels of paper while the map above or below it folds away. A red band crosses the heading of the open leg, and the heading is drawn a second time in white where the band has reached. The maps are made up: a height for every point, contour lines found with marching squares, woods, a shore and a path with a tick at each kilometre. Each <option> is a leg.

Order summary

One <details>. Closed, it shows the total and a row of pictures. Open, each picture goes to the start of its own line in a list, one after another, and the names and prices come in after them. The list, the prices and the totals are the element's own content, drawn as its picture. The three pictures are drawn by the canvas. The sums come from the <option> children and the shipping and vat attributes.

Bus stop timetable

Three radios for the days and a <dl> of departures for each. The paper tab slides to the checked day, and the day names are drawn twice: white on the black strip, and inverted with a filter where the paper tab is. The timetables are laid out side by side by the canvas and slide across. All three stay laid out, and the two that aren't checked are inert. Each <option> is a day, with its departures in data-times.

Kinetic poster

Four radios and an <output>. The figure is the output's own text, set 240 pixels high, and its picture is stretched so that the ink of the figures fills the poster from edge to edge whatever the number is. When the period changes, the old figure is pressed flat against the top while the new one grows from the bottom. The names of the tabs are labels, drawn at 0.62 of their width to make a condensed face out of an ordinary one.

How it works

Each control is a custom element on the same base class as the meters and ranges. Its shadow root holds a canvas with content="drawable", and the native elements are children of that canvas. The canvas calls drawElementImage() for each one, which draws its picture and puts its hit region in the same place.

A <details> is hard to animate from a picture, because a closed one has no content in its picture. Opening is easy: the element opens at once and the canvas clips its picture to a growing height. For closing, the control cancels the click on the <summary>, draws less of the picture each frame, and removes the open attribute when nothing of the content is left. The form value changes at the click. For about a third of a second the element is open while the control says it's closed. If something else opens or closes the element, its toggle event tells the control and the drawing jumps to match.

Each <details> is drawn whole inside a clip, so its hit region is larger than what you see of it. The sections are drawn from the top down, and where two hit regions overlap the element drawn last answers, so the heading below takes the taps over the hidden part.

The tabs are radios with no alpha under drawn labels. The bus timetables are three <dl>s drawn side by side at an offset that follows a spring. The poster's figure is one drawElementImage() with a width and height worked out from where the ink of the text is, measured with measureText() on a second context with the output's computed font. All five stop asking for frames when nothing moves.

Live checks

Findings

  • A canvas can draw a <details> closing if the element stays open until the drawing is done. 140 ms after a click the first section was drawn about half open and still had its open attribute. It lost it when the drawing reached zero.
  • A paint can come before the toggle event. When a script set open on a closed section, the canvas painted first, and my first version saw an open element it was drawing shut and closed it again. The control now remembers the state it last gave the element.
  • The hidden part of a clipped element still has a hit region, and the element drawn after it wins. The point 30 units under the drawn edge of a half-closed section answered the heading below it.
  • An element wider than its canvas is drawn whole. The output with "58,204" is 902 by 240 CSS pixels inside a control 360 wide. Drawn at 0.36 of its width and 1.10 of its height, the figures were sharp in the test browser.
  • A filter turns one picture into two colours. The headings of the walk and the names of the days are each drawn twice from the same element, the second time inside a clip with brightness(0) invert(1) or invert(1).
  • inert elements are still drawn. The two timetables that aren't checked are inert, they slide past during a change, and the point in the panel answered only the checked day's list.
  • The bottle and the pictures of the order are far from the originals. Theirs look like photographs. Mine are gradients and paths drawn on a plain canvas.
  • Not verified: everything on a phone, what a screen reader says while a section is open in the element and closed in the drawing, find in page opening a section, and the fonts. The originals use condensed and Didone faces, and the test browser had neither.
